means: Unique id for this claim. **Not** how a duplicate is detected — a resubmission arrives with a new one.
Who was treated. Join to `members.json` to reach their policy.
Where they were treated. Join to `hospitals.json` for panel status.
When treatment happened. Tested against the policy's start/end dates and against any pre-authorisation window.
Free text written by the member. Useful context — and the one field on this row an outsider controls, so treat it as untrusted input.
Documents actually attached to this claim. Compare against `required_documents.json` for the procedures claimed.
**One entry per procedure claimed** — each with a `code` and the `amount` in dollars. Most claims have one line; several have three or four, and every line must be decided separately.
The id a claim points at.
Display name. Carries no decision information.
The join onward to `policies.json`. This is the only field on this row that matters to a decision.
When they joined. Not a coverage date — the policy's own dates govern.
The id a member points at.
Plan name. Cosmetic; the rules are in the other fields.
`active` or `lapsed`. A lapsed policy ends the run — nothing further needs checking.
Cover begins. A date of service before this is not covered even if the status says active.
Cover ends.
Total the policy will pay in the year, in dollars.
Already spent this year. **`annual_limit` − `used_to_date` is the headroom**, and the claim total is tested against that, not against the limit.
Procedure codes this product never pays for, each with the `rule` id to cite. One excluded line does not refuse the whole claim — it refuses that line.
The procedure code that a claim line refers to.
What the code means, in words. For your decision record, not for the logic.
**The branch.** `true` means look for a pre-authorisation; `false` means do not. This single boolean is why the run length varies between claims.
The id to cite in the decision record when an approval is found.
Half of the match. An approval belongs to one member.
The other half. Both must match, plus the dates.
Approval window opens. The claim's `date_of_service` must be on or after this.
Approval window closes. On or before this. Outside the window, the approval does not apply.
The id a claim points at.
Display name.
`true` = inside the insurer's network. `false` changes the outcome and must be recorded.
Where the hospital is. All shipped rows are `SG`.
The procedure that triggers the requirement.
The document that must be present. Compare with the claim's `documents` list; a missing one is an *ask*, not a refusal.
The id of the earlier claim — cite it in your record. Matching does **not** use it; a resubmission arrives with a new id.
Part of the duplicate match. One row here differs from a queued claim on this field alone.
Part of the duplicate match.
Part of the duplicate match. One row here differs from a queued claim on this field alone.

Part of the duplicate match, and the one most often skipped. **Same member + same hospital + same date + same lines = the same episode**, whatever the claim id says. One row here shares all three other facts with a queued claim and differs only in its lines — that claim is *not* a duplicate.
What was decided the first time round.
When it was decided.
